traveler: Johann Georg Faust (Georgius Sabellicus Faustus junior)
title: The Man Under the Chapbook: an astrologer's paper trail and the flight that replaced it
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Knittlingen, the first claimed birthplace
stops.date_confidence: tradition; no birth record survives and scholars split between c. 1466 and c. 1480/81, so month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: Knittlingen in the duchy of Wurttemberg claims him. No baptismal register names him, no parents are recorded, no year is fixed. The claim rests on local memory and on Melanchthon's remark, passed down by his student Manlius, that he knew a Faustus of Kundling, a small town not far from his own homeland. Two other towns claim the same child, and German reference works add Simmern and Salzwedel to the field. Five places are named for the birth of one man, and not one of them produces a document.
sources: Local Knittlingen tradition; Faust-Museum Knittlingen
Johannes Manlius, Locorum Communium Collectanea (Basel, 1563; German edition 1565)
Frank Baron, Doctor Faustus: From History to Legend (1978/1992)
suggested_refs: The Altes Rathaus and Alte Lateinschule of Knittlingen, housing the Faust-Museum and Faust-Archiv

stops.name: Helmstadt, the second claim
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from a 1528 document; Baron's identification, contested, and the year is a placeholder
stops.campa: Helmstadt near Heidelberg claims him too, and on better paper than Knittlingen. In 1528 the prior Kilian Leib writes the name into his weather diary as Georgius Faustus helmstet, and Frank Baron reads that form as a place of origin. A competing account has assigned the same epithet to Mutianus Rufus's letter of 1513; that letter reads Helmitheus Hedelbergensis instead. Two documents, fifteen years apart, and only the later one points at this village. The atlas leaves both towns standing.
sources: Kilian Leib, Wettertagebuch, Kloster Rebdorf, 1528
Frank Baron, Doctor Faustus: From History to Legend
de.wikipedia, 'Helmstadt-Bargen'
suggested_refs: Helmstadt-Bargen in the Rhein-Neckar-Kreis, Baron's candidate for the Helmstet of the Rebdorf diary

stops.name: Stadtroda, the third claim
stops.date_confidence: tradition transmitted at two removes; no date attaches to it at all
stops.campa: Philipp Melanchthon, as his student Manlius reports him, names Roda near Weimar. The same chain of transmission elsewhere yields Kundling, and Kundling is read as Knittlingen. A single reported table talk thus supplies two incompatible birthplaces three hundred kilometres apart, and the atlas pins both. Nothing in the Thuringian record answers. Roda keeps its claim on Melanchthon's name alone. Melanchthon was born at Bretten, five kilometres from Knittlingen and three hundred from Roda.
sources: Johannes Manlius, Locorum communium collectanea, Basel 1563, recording Melanchthon's table talk
suggested_refs: Stadtroda in Thuringia, the Roda of the Melanchthon tradition

stops.name: Heidelberg, a magister named Helmstetter
stops.date_confidence: attested for Helmstetter's matriculation year; the identification with Faust is disputed and undecided
stops.campa: A Georgius Helmstetter matriculates here in 1483, is made baccalaureus on the twelfth of July 1484 and magister artium on the first of March 1487. The university keeps its books well. Whether this graduate is the man who later signs himself Faustus of Heidelberg, no document says. Baron thinks so; others do not. Thirty-one years after Helmstetter takes his magister degree, Martin Luther comes to this town to defend his theses before the Augustinians. The registers that date one graduate to the day hold nothing at all under the name Faust.
sources: Heidelberg University matriculation and promotion records, 1483, 1484, 1487
Frank Baron, Doctor Faustus: From History to Legend
martin_luther.journey.json (Heidelberg Disputation, 1518)
suggested_refs: The Heidelberg matriculation register for 1483 and the promotion lists of 1484 and 1487

stops.name: Krakow, the school of the art
stops.date_confidence: tradition only; no matriculation record survives and no year is given by any source
stops.campa: Manlius has Melanchthon say that the man from Kundling learned the magic art at Krakow, where the university teaches astrology openly and where a reputation for teaching more than astrology is already fixed. No matriculation record carries the name. The claim travels regardless. It attaches itself to the Polish legend of Pan Twardowski, the scholar who signs with the devil, and it supplies the wandering German with a school for a science no faculty admits to teaching.
sources: Johannes Manlius, Locorum communium collectanea, 1563, relaying Melanchthon
Jagiellonian University matriculation records, negative
suggested_refs: The Collegium Maius of the Jagiellonian University, Krakow, the astrological faculty of the legend

segments.name: The First Name in the Record

stops.name: Gelnhausen, the first trace of the name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: At the imperial town on the Kinzig a wandering performer offers magic tricks and casts horoscopes, and calls himself Faust. This is the first time anyone writes the name down. He is already doing what he will be recorded doing for the next three decades: selling prediction to whoever will pay, in a town he does not stay in. Trithemius will hear the tales the following year and remember passing near enough to catch them. Everything before this stop is claim; everything after it is a paper trail with holes in it.
sources: Gelnhausen municipal record cited by Frank Baron
Johannes Trithemius, letter to Johannes Virdung, 20 August 1507
suggested_refs: The Kaiserpfalz of Gelnhausen, the imperial palace above the Kinzig

stops.name: Wurzburg, Trithemius writes to Virdung
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: From the Schottenkloster St. Jakob, which he has led since resigning Sponheim the year before, Johannes Trithemius warns the astrologer Johannes Virdung of Hasfurt against a vagrant styling himself fountain of necromancers and second magus. The abbot reports that the man boasted he could reproduce all the miracles of Christ at will, and calls him a fool rather than a philosopher. Within a year Trithemius will be teaching alchemy in this same city to a young Swiss who takes the name Paracelsus. This letter is the earliest description of the man that survives anywhere.
stops.quote: Sabellicus boasted blasphemously of his powers, even claiming that he could easily reproduce all the miracles of Christ.
stops.quote_source: Johannes Trithemius, letter to Johannes Virdung of Hasfurt, 20 August 1507, as rendered in secondary literature; the letter itself was not reachable for this atlas
sources: Johannes Trithemius, letter to Johannes Virdung, 20 August 1507
E. M. Butler, The Fortunes of Faust (1952)
paracelsus.journey.json (Wurzburg, Trithemius as teacher, 1508)
suggested_refs: The Schottenkloster St. Jakob at Wurzburg, Trithemius's abbey from 1506

stops.name: Bad Kreuznach, the schoolmaster who fled
stops.date_confidence: attested by the 1507 letter; month and day of the episode unrecorded
stops.campa: Trithemius reports that the man held a schoolmaster's post here, secured through the patronage of the knight Franz von Sickingen, and that he fled the town after being accused of sodomy with the boys in his charge. The accusation will follow the name: twenty-five years later a Nuremberg mayor still writes sodomite beside nigromancer. A house in the town is shown as the Faust-Haus and dated to 1492, but the letter that is the only real evidence names no house, and local historians doubt the date.
sources: Johannes Trithemius, letter to Johannes Virdung, 1507
Bad Kreuznach local historical tradition, 'Faust Haus'
suggested_refs: The Latin school of Kreuznach, the post Sickingen's patronage obtained

stops.name: Ebernburg, the patron above the Nahe
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Trithemius names Sickingen but not the castle, and the pin is reconstruction
stops.campa: Franz von Sickingen holds his family seat on the spur above the Nahe, and a knight's word puts a wandering chiromancer into a schoolroom five kilometres downriver. Trithemius names the patron and not the place. Sickingen will later shelter Ulrich von Hutten here and earn the castle the name Herberge der Gerechtigkeit, inn of righteousness; in 1507 his patronage extends to a man his own century calls a fraud. The pin is inferred from where Sickingen lived, and no document puts Faust on this rock.
sources: Inferred from Sickingen's known residence; not stated in Trithemius's letter
de.wikipedia, 'Ebernburg'
suggested_refs: Burg Ebernburg above the Nahe, seat of Franz von Sickingen

stops.name: Erfurt, the chiromancer at the inn
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the letter is undated within it
stops.campa: Conrad Mutianus Rufus writes to Heinrich Urbanus that eight days ago a palm-reader came to Erfurt calling himself Georgius Faustus Helmitheus Hedelbergensis, and that the man is a mere braggart and a fool. The humanists of the Gotha circle keep a settled contempt for fortune-tellers and spend it freely. Twelve years before this, Martin Luther matriculated in this town; eight years before it, he entered the Augustinian cloister here. By 1513 Luther is at Wittenberg lecturing on the Psalms, and the two men never meet.
stops.quote: Vor acht Tagen kam ein Chiromant nach Erfurt, namens Georgius Faustus Helmitheus Hedelbergensis, ein bloßer Prahler und Narr.
stops.quote_source: Conrad Mutianus Rufus, letter to Heinrich Urbanus, 1513, in the German rendering carried by de.wikipedia; the original letter and a scholarly edition were both unreachable
sources: Conrad Mutianus Rufus, letter to Heinrich Urbanus, 1513
martin_luther.journey.json (Erfurt matriculation 1501, cloister 1505)
suggested_refs: The inns of the Erfurt market quarter, where Mutianus overheard the chiromancer

stops.name: Kloster Maulbronn, the abbot's colleague
stops.date_confidence: tradition recorded a century and a half after the fact; the 1516 date comes from the later register, not from any contemporary paper
stops.campa: A seventeenth-century Wurttemberg household register compiled by Philipp Jacob Zeiter calls Abbot Johann Entenfuss the collega of a Dr. Fausten, and the monastery's building works of 1516 thereby acquire a magician. No sixteenth-century paper says so. The Cistercians keep excellent accounts and none of them names him. A tower in the precinct is called the Faustturm on the strength of that register alone, which is to say on the strength of a note written long after the visit it records.
sources: Philipp Jacob Zeiter, Furstlich Wurttembergisches Dienerbuch, 17th century
suggested_refs: The Faustturm in the precinct of Kloster Maulbronn

stops.name: Erfurt, the lecture on Homer
stops.date_confidence: tradition with no contemporary Erfurt record; the 1520s dating is itself a later inference
stops.campa: Later tradition, running through the Melanchthon circle to Manlius and out into local legend, has him lecturing at the university on Homer and conjuring the Homeric heroes into the hall for his students to look at. The Franciscan Konrad Klinge is said to have warned him off. No Erfurt record confirms any of it. Three centuries afterward Goethe comes to this city for his audience with Napoleon, in the same year he publishes the first part of his Faust.
sources: Johannes Manlius, Locorum communium collectanea, 1563; Erfurt local tradition
goethe_full.journey.json (Erfurt, 2 October 1808)
suggested_refs: The Collegium Maius of the University of Erfurt, setting of the legendary Homer lectures

stops.name: Bamberg, ten gulden for a nativity
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the court chamber accounts
stops.campa: The episcopal court chamber enters a payment: ten gulden, given and presented to doctor Faustus the philosopher, for making a nativity for my gracious lord. The gracious lord is Prince-Bishop Georg III Schenk von Limpurg. This is the clearest thing in the whole record. A bishop's treasurer, keeping books he expects to be audited, writes down the name, the title, the service and the fee. Whatever else the man is, he is at this moment a working astrologer employed at a German court and paid the going rate.
stops.quote: Item X guld[en] geben und geschenckt doctor faustus ph[ilosoph]o zuuererung hat m[einem] g[nedigen] herrn ein nativitet oder Indicium gemacht.
stops.quote_source: Bamberg episcopal Hofkammerrechnung, 1520, as excerpted on de.wikipedia; the archival record itself was not consulted
sources: Bamberg episcopal Hofkammerrechnung, 1520, cited by Frank Baron (1978)
suggested_refs: The Alte Hofhaltung at Bamberg, seat of the prince-bishop's chamber

stops.name: Kloster Rebdorf, the weather diary
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the diary entry
stops.campa: Prior Kilian Leib keeps a diary of the weather and writes into it, on the fifth of June, what Georgius Faustus helmstet has told him: that when sun and Jupiter stand in the same degree of one and the same sign, prophets are born. The same entry records the visitor claiming the rank of a Johanniter, a Knight Hospitaller, which he assuredly is not. Here is the man's own reasoning, in two lines, preserved by accident between notes on rain. It is very nearly all of his thought that survives anywhere.
stops.quote: He stated that when sun and Jupiter occupy same degree of zodiac sign, prophets are born.
stops.quote_source: Kilian Leib, Wettertagebuch, Kloster Rebdorf, entry of 5 June 1528
sources: Kilian Leib, Wettertagebuch, 1528
de.wikipedia, 'Kloster Rebdorf'
suggested_refs: Kloster Rebdorf near Eichstatt and the surviving weather diary of Prior Kilian Leib

stops.name: Ingolstadt, told to spend his pennies elsewhere
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; English-language summaries give 27 June, the council minute reads the Wednesday after St. Vitus, 17 June
stops.campa: Twelve days after Rebdorf, on the Wednesday after the feast of Saint Vitus, the city council orders one who calls himself Dr. Jorg Faustus of Heidelberg to spend his pennies somewhere else. It is an expulsion phrased as a municipal courtesy, and the reason understood behind it is fortune-telling. He has been in the town long enough to be noticed and not long enough to be tolerated. This is the rhythm of the documented life: paid at Bamberg, banished at Ingolstadt, moving on in either case.
stops.quote: Am Mittwoch nach viti 1528 ist einem der sich genant Dr. Jörg Faustus von Heidelberg gesagt, dass er seinen Pfennig anderswo verzehre.
stops.quote_source: Ingolstadt Ratsprotokoll, 17 June 1528, as excerpted on de.wikipedia; the city archive was not consulted
sources: Ingolstadt Ratsprotokolle, 17 June 1528
de.wikipedia, 'Johann Georg Faust'
suggested_refs: The Ingolstadt council minutes for June 1528

stops.name: Nuremberg, safe conduct refused
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the mayor's note is undated within it
stops.campa: The junior mayor writes an instruction for the gatekeepers of the imperial free city: refuse safe conduct to Doctor Fausto, the great sodomite and nigromancer, and signs it Burgermeister Junior. The accusation Trithemius recorded at Kreuznach in 1507 has travelled twenty-five years and is now municipal fact. Three years before this note Paracelsus stood in this same city and signed his adopted name for the first time. Nuremberg tolerates one wandering doctor and shuts its gate on the other.
stops.quote: Doctor Fausto, dem grossen Sodomitten und Nigromantico zu furr, glait ablainen. Burg[ermeister] Ju[ni]or.
sources: Staatsarchiv Nurnberg, Nurnberger Ratserlasse Nr. 810
paracelsus.journey.json (Nuremberg, 1529)
suggested_refs: The Nurnberger Ratserlasse in the Staatsarchiv Nurnberg, Nr. 810

segments.name: The Last Years on the Record

stops.name: Augsburg, the horoscope for the Welser fleet
stops.date_confidence: inference only; no source states where or when the horoscope was cast, and the year is read backward from the expedition's departure
stops.campa: The Welser banking house governs its grant of Venezuela from offices in this city and fits out expeditions for it. Somewhere before the fleet sails, a philosopher named Faust casts a figure for the venture and predicts hardship. Where he cast it, no document says; Augsburg is the guess that fits the geography. One account places the casting at Bad Mergentheim instead, on no evidence whatever. The only evidence that the casting happened at all is a letter written six years afterward from the Caribbean coast.
sources: Inferred from Philipp von Hutten's letter of 15 January 1540; casting location not stated in any source
suggested_refs: The Welser house at Augsburg, seat of the company that held the Venezuela grant

stops.name: Munster, in the year of the Anabaptist kingdom
stops.date_confidence: reported for the day in modern scholarship; the underlying record was not reachable and the pin follows the city centre, no site being named
stops.campa: Modern scholarship reports him present in the Westphalian city on the twenty-fifth of June 1535, as the bishop's forces finish the Anabaptist kingdom and the cages are made ready for the bodies of its prophets. It is among the last dated sightings of the living man. The record behind the date could not be opened for this atlas, and no source names a street or a house. He appears, in the single line that survives, in a city that has just spent more than a year under siege over the question of baptism.
sources: Contemporary record cited in modern Faust scholarship, date 25 June 1535; primary source not reachable
suggested_refs: The Prinzipalmarkt and St. Lambert's church at Munster, where the cages still hang

stops.name: Tubingen, Camerarius on the astrologer
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the letter
stops.campa: Joachim Camerarius, holding his chair here from 1535, writes to Daniel Stibar about Faust's astrology and dismisses it as the emptiest superstition. The letter is worth more than its verdict: it shows that Stibar follows the man's predictions, and that a professor of Greek at a good university expects his correspondent to know at once whom he means. One modern reading has Camerarius respecting Faust as a genuine astrologer. The letter does not say that, and both readings stand in print.
sources: Joachim Camerarius, letter to Daniel Stibar, 1536
de.wikipedia, 'Johann Georg Faust', characterising the judgment as nichtigsten Aberglauben
suggested_refs: The Alte Aula of the University of Tubingen, where Camerarius held his chair from 1535 to 1541

stops.name: Korbach, an uncorroborated passage
stops.date_confidence: single late chronicle, flagged by later scholarship as unverified against contemporary records
stops.campa: Daniel Prasser's Waldeck chronicle puts him passing through the Hessian town. Nothing else does. Later scholarship marks the notice as uncorroborated and leaves it standing, and so does the atlas: one chronicler, writing after the fact, in a region that produces no other Faust paper. Dropping the weak notices would make the strong ones look tidier than they are. Most of what is known about him is a line of exactly this kind in somebody's book, with nothing standing behind it.
sources: Daniel Prasser, Waldeckische Chronik, later 16th century
suggested_refs: The Waldeckische Chronik of Daniel Prasser, sole source for the Korbach notice

stops.name: Worms, the physician's complaint
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; the episodes it describes are undated
stops.campa: Philipp Begardi, city physician, publishes his Index Sanitatis and puts into it a formal complaint about a travelling healer: many people came to him and were deceived, his promises were large and his results were nothing. Begardi is not writing legend and has no interest in devils. He is filing a professional warning about a competitor who has taken money from his patients. This is the last securely dated notice of the man alive, and what it amounts to is a consumer complaint.
stops.quote: Many complained they were deceived by him; his promises were great but results deceptive.
sources: Philipp Begardi, Index Sanitatis, Worms, 1539
suggested_refs: Begardi's Index Sanitatis, printed at Worms in 1539

stops.name: Coro, the letter from Venezuela
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Philipp von Hutten, knight and imperial councillor, writes home from the Welser colony on the Caribbean coast that the philosopher Faust had not been far wrong about the year: they have had a very bad one. The man himself is dead or dying in the Breisgau as the letter is written, and his name has crossed the Atlantic in the mouth of a conquistador. Of all the surviving testimony about him this is the only piece written by somebody who wanted the prediction to be true.
stops.quote: The philosopher Faust nearly predicted it; we had a very bad year.
stops.quote_source: Philipp von Hutten, letter from Coro, Venezuela, 15 January 1540
sources: Philipp von Hutten, letter of 15 January 1540
suggested_refs: Coro on the Venezuelan coast, seat of the Welser colony

stops.name: Staufen im Breisgau, the death at the Lowen
stops.date_confidence: year disputed between 1540 and 1541; no primary record fixes it, and month and day are defaulted
stops.campa: In the lordship of Staufen, lodging at the inn called Zum Lowen and working for a local nobleman, he dies. The town will say it was an explosion in an alchemical experiment and will hang an inscription on the wall to say so. The chronicle nearest the event says only that he died miserably. Some sources give 1540 and some 1541, and nothing decides between them. No grave, no marker, no burial entry has ever been found for him anywhere. The end of the documented life is a hole in the parish books.
sources: Local Staufen tradition and the inscription at the Gasthaus zum Lowen
Froben Christoph von Zimmern, Zimmerische Chronik, c. 1564-1566, for the bare fact of the death
suggested_refs: The Gasthaus zum Lowen at Staufen im Breisgau and its inscription

segments.name: The Witnesses Who Wrote Him Down

stops.name: Basel, Gast at table with him
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; the dinner it reports is undated and may never have happened
stops.campa: The reformer Johann Gast prints his Sermones Convivales and claims in them to have dined with Faust, and to have heard afterward of a dreadful death and of a dog that vanished. He reports that the corpse kept turning its face to the ground however often the bystanders laid it on its back. Nothing outside Gast corroborates any of it. Twenty years before, Paracelsus burned Avicenna's Canon in this city and fled it by night; the Rhine university towns collect such men and then write them up as warnings.
sources: Johann Gast, Sermones Convivales (Basel, 1548)
paracelsus.journey.json (Basel, 1526-1528)
suggested_refs: Johann Gast's Sermones Convivales, printed at Basel in 1548

stops.name: Wittenberg, Melanchthon's disgraceful beast
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1563 in Latin, 1565 in German; the remarks themselves are undated and reach print after Melanchthon's death in 1560
stops.campa: Johannes Manlius publishes his teacher's table talk at Basel, and Melanchthon in it says he knew a Faustus of Kundling, a small town not far from his own homeland, who had learned the magic art at Krakow. Elsewhere in the same tradition he calls him a most disgraceful beast and a sewer of many devils. Melanchthon has taught in this town beside Martin Luther for four decades and has been three years dead when the book appears; a generation later Giordano Bruno will lecture here too.
stops.quote: Ich hab einen gekennet / mit nammen Faustus von Kundling (ist ein kleines stettlein / nicht weit von meinem Vatterland) derselbige da er zu Crockaw in die Schul gieng / da hatte er die Zauberey gelernet...
stops.quote_source: Johannes Manlius, Locorum Communium Collectanea, Basel 1563, pp. 42f; this German wording belongs to the German edition of 1565, the 1563 volume being in Latin
sources: Johannes Manlius, Locorum Communium Collectanea, Basel 1563 (Latin), German edition 1565
martin_luther.journey.json (Wittenberg stops with Melanchthon, 1517-1546)
giordano_bruno.journey.json (Wittenberg, 1586-1588)
suggested_refs: The Leucorea, the University of Wittenberg, Melanchthon's chair for four decades

stops.name: Staufen im Breisgau, what the chronicle actually says
stops.date_confidence: composition dated c. 1564-1566; the entry itself carries no date
stops.campa: Froben Christoph von Zimmern, compiling his family chronicle, writes that Faust died ellengclichen, miserably, in the lordship of Staufen about the time of the Reichstag, and that many believed the evil spirit had taken him. That is the whole of it. No explosion, no alchemical experiment, no mutilated body. Those details are attached later, by the town and by Gast respectively, and then read back into the chronicle by people who have not opened it. This is the earliest account of the death there is.
stops.quote: He died miserably; many believed the evil spirit took his soul.
stops.quote_source: Froben Christoph von Zimmern, Zimmerische Chronik, c. 1564-1566, in English paraphrase; the chronicle was not opened directly for this atlas
sources: Froben Christoph von Zimmern, Zimmerische Chronik, c. 1564-1566
suggested_refs: The Zimmerische Chronik, earliest narrative source for Faust's death

stops.name: Nuremberg, the last men who claim to have known him
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to the year; the pin follows Camerarius's known base, since the source names no site
stops.campa: Philipp Camerarius, jurist and son of the professor who dismissed Faust's astrology at Tubingen, publishes his Operae Horarum Subcisivarum and reports that he has spoken with people who knew the man personally. Sixty years after the death, a witness would have to be eighty to have met the man, and would have had the chapbook to read for fifteen of those years. Testimony and invention can no longer be told apart. The record names no place for this; the pin is reconstruction from the writer's residence.
sources: Philipp Camerarius, Operae Horarum Subcisivarum (1602)
suggested_refs: Philipp Camerarius's Operae Horarum Subcisivarum, 1602

segments.name: The Chapbook and Its Grand Tour

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Spies prints the Historia
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: Johann Spies puts out an anonymous book called the Historia von D. Johann Fausten, and the man is finished. The pact is invented here, and the twenty-four years, and the flight over Christendom, and the dismemberment at midnight. The Historia also awards him a Wittenberg doctorate in theology that no matriculation register records. From this year forward every Faust is this Faust; the astrologer of the Bamberg accounts survives only in archives that nobody reads again for two hundred years.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten (Johann Spies, Frankfurt am Main, 1587)
suggested_refs: Johann Spies's 1587 Historia von D. Johann Fausten, the first printed Faustbook

stops.name: Wittenberg, the house on Collegienstrasse
stops.date_confidence: undated local tradition attached to the chapbook after 1587; the date shown is the chapbook's, not the tradition's
stops.campa: The chapbook sets his study and his pact in Wittenberg, and Wittenberg obliges with a house. A building on Collegienstrasse is remembered as his lodging and as the place where the spirit was bound; a plaque marks it now, of a date nobody has established. Not one sixteenth-century document places the living man in this town. Spies printed at Frankfurt and set the pact at Wittenberg, where the century's loudest argument about the price of a soul had been conducted for seventy years.
sources: Wittenberg local tradition; Gedenktafel, Collegienstrasse 31
Historia von D. Johann Fausten, 1587
suggested_refs: The Fausthaus and its plaque at Collegienstrasse 31, Lutherstadt Wittenberg

stops.name: Leipzig, the barrel ride at Auerbachs Keller
stops.date_confidence: undated legend, fixed in print by the 1587 Faustbuch; the date shown is the book's
stops.campa: In the vaulted cellar under the Auerbachshof the legend has him ride a wine barrel up the stairs and out into the street while the students stare after him. Two painted panels in the vault keep the scene. The story is in the chapbook and in no archive at all, and it is the one Faust episode that anybody in Germany can still recite. Goethe drinks in this cellar as a student in the 1760s and puts the room, the students and the barrel into his play.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten, Frankfurt, 1587
goethe_full.journey.json (Leipzig student years)
suggested_refs: The painted panels of the barrel ride in Auerbachs Keller, Leipzig

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the almanacs at the Romerberg
stops.date_confidence: legend; the Faustbuch places him at the fair and no record does, the date shown being the book's
stops.campa: The chapbook has him among the booksellers of the Frankfurt fair, selling almanacs and prognostications to the trading public. The book that says so is itself printed in this city and sold at that same fair, which is a neat piece of advertising. Two centuries later Goethe grows up a few streets from the Romerberg, reads the alchemists in a sickroom at nineteen and builds a furnace to look for the stone. The fair is still running, and it still sells books.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten, Frankfurt, 1587
goethe_full.journey.json (Frankfurt, alchemy, 1769)
suggested_refs: The Romerberg and the booksellers' stalls of the Frankfurt fair

stops.name: Rome, the Pope's table
stops.date_confidence: legend, fixed in the 1587 Faustbuch; the date shown is the book's
stops.campa: Carried invisible by his spirit into the Vatican palace, the chapbook Faust snatches dishes from the papal banquet and boxes the pontiff's ears before vanishing. It is Lutheran comedy, printed in a Lutheran city for readers who enjoy watching the Pope robbed at his own table. Thirteen years after the Historia appears, the Roman Inquisition burns Giordano Bruno in the Campo de' Fiori for opinions that include the practice of magic. The joke and the fire belong to one century.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten, 1587, chapter on the journey to Rome
giordano_bruno.journey.json (Rome, 1600)
suggested_refs: The Vatican banqueting halls of the Faustbuch's Rome chapter

stops.name: Naples and Vesuvius, the mouth of the mountain
stops.date_confidence: legend, fixed in the 1587 Faustbuch; the date shown is the book's
stops.campa: The grand tour brings him to Naples and to the burning crater above it, where the chapbook has him look down into the fire and take its measure. Hell is a geographical destination in this book, reachable by air, and Vesuvius is the nearest available mouth. The Faust of the archives never left the German lands so far as any record shows. The Faust of the print shops crosses the entire known world in a single chapter and is home again the same night.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten, Frankfurt, 1587
suggested_refs: The crater of Vesuvius above Naples, station of the chapbook's aerial tour

stops.name: Venice, the conjuror before the crowds
stops.date_confidence: legend, fixed in the 1587 Faustbuch; the date shown is the book's
stops.campa: The Historia sets him displaying his arts to the wonder of the Venetian crowds, one stage of a flight across Christendom that touches every city a German reader of 1587 has heard of. The itinerary is a list of famous places rather than a route: it goes where reputation goes. The historical man sold horoscopes at Bamberg for ten gulden and was thrown out of Ingolstadt for doing it. His double performs free, for everyone, in the richest city in Europe.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten, Frankfurt, 1587
suggested_refs: The Piazza San Marco, stage of the Faustbuch's Venetian conjuring

stops.name: Vienna, the visions at the imperial court
stops.date_confidence: legend with no supporting court record; the date shown is the chapbook's
stops.campa: Legend brings him before the emperor at the Hofburg to conjure visions for the court's amusement, and later dramatists elaborate the scene into an audience with Charles V and an apparition of Alexander the Great. The imperial chancery keeps voluminous records and none of them contains him. A man refused entry at the gate of Nuremberg in 1532 is given, in print, the ear of the Holy Roman Emperor. Charles V, whom the dramatists choose for the scene, had been crowned two years before that refusal.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten, 1587, and later dramatic elaborations
suggested_refs: The Hofburg at Vienna, setting of the legendary imperial audience

stops.name: Paris, the cities of the west
stops.date_confidence: legend, fixed in the 1587 Faustbuch; the date shown is the book's
stops.campa: The aerial tour carries him over Paris among the cities of France and the Low Countries, surveyed from above and named in a list. Nothing happens here in the book; the city is furniture. Three centuries later Charles Gounod's Faust opens in this city and runs for decades, and Paris becomes, for the nineteenth century, the place where the legend is chiefly sung. The chapbook flew over it without stopping, and the atlas keeps the stop for the flight path rather than the event.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten, Frankfurt, 1587
Reception history: Gounod's Faust, Paris, 1859, external to the corpus
suggested_refs: Charles Gounod's Faust, premiered at Paris in 1859

stops.name: Constantinople, the Sultan's palace
stops.date_confidence: legend with no Ottoman corroboration; the date shown is the chapbook's
stops.campa: The chapbook sends him invisible into the Sultan's court, where he haunts the harem and mocks the throne. The Ottoman archives are extensive and record no such visitor. This is as far east as a German Protestant book of 1587 cares to travel, and it goes there to humiliate the Turk exactly as it humiliated the Pope at Rome. Suleiman had died in 1566 and the siege of Vienna was within living memory; of all foreign matters, the Turkish wars were the one every German reader followed.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten, Frankfurt, 1587
suggested_refs: Hagia Sophia and the Sultan's palace, stations of the Faustbuch's eastern flight

stops.name: Cairo, down the Nile
stops.date_confidence: legend, fixed in the 1587 Faustbuch; the date shown is the book's
stops.campa: The flight follows the Nile down to Cairo and the wonders of Egypt are surveyed from the air. Egypt is where the hermetic books are supposed to have come from, and the chapbook's readers know it. He does not land and he does not read; he looks down and moves on. The hermetic books those readers thought Egyptian were written in Greek at Alexandria, and Isaac Casaubon will demonstrate it in 1614. The book that gave him twenty-four years of unlimited knowledge spends most of them on sightseeing.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten, Frankfurt, 1587
suggested_refs: The Nile and the pyramids of Giza, seen from the air in the chapbook's Egypt chapter

stops.name: Jerusalem, the turning point of the flight
stops.date_confidence: legend, fixed in the 1587 Faustbuch; the date shown is the book's
stops.campa: Over the Holy Land the spirit turns him back toward Germany. This is the furthest point of the grand tour and the only station where the book holds him off: the damned man is allowed to look down at Jerusalem and no nearer. The pact has a geography as well as a term of years. In 1587 the city is Ottoman ground, and no German reaches it without the Sultan's leave. He has robbed the Pope and mocked the Sultan, and here he circles once and goes home. Marlowe will cut the whole tour to a few lines; Goethe will drop it entirely.
sources: Historia von D. Johann Fausten, Frankfurt, 1587

suggested_refs: The Temple Mount at Jerusalem, furthest station of the chapbook's flight

stops.name: London, the English Faustbook
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1592; a lost earlier printing is posited by some scholars but none survives or is attested, and summaries giving 1587 or 1588 are wrong
stops.campa: A translator signing himself P.F. Gent. publishes The Historie of the Damnable Life and Deserved Death of Doctor John Faustus, five years after the German original and not one year after it, whatever the summaries say. Christopher Marlowe reads it and writes his play. The English book is the only text in the entire dossier that puts extended speech into Faust's mouth, and every word of that speech is fiction, composed at second hand by men who never saw him.
stops.quote: I, Johannes Faustus, Doctor, do openly acknowledge with mine own hand, to the greater force and strengthening of this Letter, that siththence I began to study and speculate the course and order of the Elements, I have not found through the gift that is given me from above, any such learning and wisdom, that can bring me to my desires.
stops.quote_source: The Historie of the Damnable Life and Deserved Death of Doctor John Faustus (London, 1592), chapter VI, the text of the pact; Project Gutenberg ebook 70359
sources: P.F. Gent (trans.), The Historie of the Damnable Life and Deserved Death of Doctor John Faustus (London, 1592), Project Gutenberg ebook 70359
suggested_refs: The 1592 English Faust Book, source of Marlowe's Doctor Faustus

stops.name: Prague, the Faust House on Karlovo namesti
stops.date_confidence: undated civic legend attached to the building's earlier alchemical tenants; the year shown is a placeholder in Rudolf II's reign
stops.campa: A Gothic house on Charles Square is called the Faust House, because alchemists lodged in it under Rudolf II and because a legend has one of them vanish through the roof, leaving a hole that would not stay mended. The alchemist gets conflated with Faust and the building keeps the name. Rudolf kept alchemists and astrologers on salary at the Hradcany, and the surviving court lists carry no Faust. John Dee and Edward Kelley worked at Rudolf's court in fact rather than in legend, and no document connects Faust to Bohemia at all.
sources: Prague civic legend attached to the Faust House on Karlovo namesti
QUEUE.md, the Trithemius-Dee-Fludd occult thread
suggested_refs: The Faust House on Karlovo namesti, Prague, and its alchemical tenants under Rudolf II

stops.name: Wittenberg, Neumann argues that he existed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: Johann Georg Neumann publishes the Disquisitio historica de Fausto praestigiatore, the first attempt to prove by scholarship that a real Faust once walked around, against contemporaries who have decided by now that the whole thing was invented. Ninety-six years after Spies, the chapbook has worked so thoroughly that the man underneath it must be argued back into existence. The archives that would settle it are sitting in Bamberg and Nuremberg and Ingolstadt, unread.
sources: Johann Georg Neumann, Disquisitio historica de Fausto praestigiatore (Wittenberg, 1683)
suggested_refs: Neumann's Disquisitio historica de Fausto praestigiatore, 1683

stops.name: Kloster Maulbronn, the tower named for him
stops.date_confidence: the naming tradition is of undetermined date, later than the 1516 visit it commemorates; the year shown is a placeholder
stops.campa: A tower in the monastery precinct is called the Faustturm. It commemorates a visit for which the only evidence is a household register compiled a century and a half afterward, calling Abbot Entenfuss the colleague of a Dr. Fausten. The stone is real and the visit is not documented. Here is the standard construction of the whole afterlife: the tradition raises a monument, and the monument is afterward produced as evidence for the tradition. The Cistercian accounts for 1516 name no Faust at all.
sources: Local Maulbronn tradition attached to the Faustturm
Philipp Jacob Zeiter, Furstlich Wurttembergisches Dienerbuch
suggested_refs: The Faustturm at Kloster Maulbronn

stops.name: Bad Kreuznach, the house called Faust's
stops.date_confidence: local tradition of undetermined date; the 1492 building date it claims is itself doubted by local historians, and the year shown is a placeholder
stops.campa: The town shows a Faust-Haus and dates it to 1492, fifteen years before the only document that puts him in Kreuznach at all. That document is Trithemius's letter, and it names a schoolmaster's post and a flight from an accusation, not a house. Local historians say the building is later than 1500. It is a restaurant now, and the atlas marks the site as tradition rather than record. The plaque on the wall is the only document in the case that anyone can actually read.
sources: Bad Kreuznach local historical tradition, 'Faust Haus'
Johannes Trithemius, letter to Johannes Virdung, 1507
suggested_refs: The Faust-Haus at Bad Kreuznach, now a restaurant

stops.name: Knittlingen, the museum and the lost paper
stops.date_confidence: the museum is a twentieth-century foundation; the transcription is dated 1934 and its purported original to 1542
stops.campa: The Altes Rathaus and the Alte Lateinschule hold the Faust-Museum and the Faust-Archiv, and the town's identity rests on being his birthplace. In 1934 Karl Weisert makes a pencil copy of a document he dates to 1542, which he says confirms the claim. The original burns in the war. The copy is now the only witness and can be collated against nothing. Four centuries after his death, the best evidence for where he was born is a handwritten note about a paper that no longer exists.
sources: Faust-Museum Knittlingen institutional record
Karl Weisert transcription (1934), cited in Knittlingen Faust-Archiv scholarship
suggested_refs: The Faust-Museum and Faust-Archiv in the Altes Rathaus and Alte Lateinschule, Knittlingen
